passage:
The power went out at 4 pm in the middle of Amandeep's video call, and the laptop battery showed nineteen percent. On the screen, Jatin's face was red. "You breached the delivery terms. My lawyer will send a notice tomorrow."

Amandeep's chest went hot. The first reply that came to mind was a nasty one. Instead: "I'll look at the agreement now and reply in writing tonight. Please send me which clause you mean."

The call dropped. By torchlight, Amandeep opened the contract on the phone and found a delivery clause allowing a week's extension if the client's files arrived late. The files had arrived nine days late. Amandeep pulled up the email thread as proof, screenshotted it and saved it in a folder.

That night, on the phone's last few percent, Amandeep typed a calm message with the clause and the dates, and added, "I'd be happy to try mediation before this goes further."

Jatin answered the next morning: "Let me check."

qa.q: What was the laptop battery level when the power went out?
qa.a: The laptop battery showed nineteen percent.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling at the accusation, and what did Amandeep do about it?
qa.a: Amandeep felt angry, chest hot and tempted to reply nastily, but chose to say the agreement would be checked and a written reply sent that night.

qa.q: Why was it wise to reply in writing with the clause and dates?
qa.a: A written reply citing the clause and the email evidence stays calm and factual, and suggesting mediation avoids an expensive escalation.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the accusation?
qa.a: Jatin may honestly believe the terms were broken and feel anxious about the client, which could explain the red face and the threat, and the late files may not have been clear to Jatin.

grounding: Accused of breaching terms and threatened with legal action, Amandeep stays calm, re-reads the agreement, collects proof and replies in writing.

passage:
Subject: Re: Breach of contract and legal notice
Dear Vidya,
Thank you for your email of 3 August. I understand you're upset that the website launch was delayed, and I take that seriously.
I've re-read our agreement dated 12 May. Clause 4 says the launch date depends on receiving final content from your side. My records show the product photographs arrived on 28 July, eleven days after the agreed date. I've attached those emails, and the timeline, for your reference.
I don't believe there has been a breach on my side. But I would rather resolve this than fight about it. I can launch within five working days of today. If you still feel the agreement was broken, I'd be open to meeting with a neutral mediator before either of us involves lawyers.
I hope we can sort this out calmly.
Regards,
Reena

qa.q: When did the product photographs arrive, according to Reena's records?
qa.a: On 28 July, eleven days after the agreed date.

qa.q: How can you tell Reena is staying calm despite the threat?
qa.a: Reena feels the weight of the threat but stays composed and respectful, taking Vidya's upset seriously instead of replying in anger.

qa.q: What steps did Reena take in responding to the accusation?
qa.a: Reena re-read the agreement, collected emails and a timeline, replied in writing, offered a solution, and suggested a neutral mediator.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel reading Reena's reply?
qa.a: Vidya may feel defensive at first, but the facts and the calm offer of mediation may cool the anger and make a fight seem unnecessary.

grounding: A client accuses the protagonist of breaching terms and threatens legal action; the protagonist re-reads the agreement, gathers proof, responds in writing and offers mediation.

passage: "So last month my client, Hrithik, sent me a message at midnight: 'You've broken our contract. My lawyer will be in touch.' I'm Yash, I do freelance video editing. My hands were actually shaking. My first instinct was to fire back something rude. I typed it. Then I made myself go to bed. Next morning I opened our agreement and read it line by line. It said three rounds of changes. We'd done six. I pulled out every email, every change request, with dates, and put them in one document. Then I replied, polite and short: 'Here's what our agreement says, and here's what we've done. I'm happy to finish the final cut. If we still disagree, could we try mediation first?' He went quiet for two days. Then he called, much calmer, and we sorted it out. That rude message is still in my drafts. Not sending it saved me a lot."

qa.q: How many rounds of changes did the agreement allow?
qa.a: Three rounds of changes; they had done six.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the midnight message arrived?
qa.a: Yash felt shaken and angry, hands trembling, with an urge to fire back something rude.

qa.q: Which choice helped Yash avoid an expensive fight?
qa.a: Sleeping on it, re-reading the agreement, collecting dated emails, and replying politely in writing with an offer of mediation.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt after reading Yash's reply?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt less sure of his accusation and calmer, which is why he called two days later to sort it out.

grounding: A client accuses the protagonist of breaching the contract and threatens action; the protagonist stays calm, re-reads the terms, gathers proof, replies in writing and suggests mediation.
